title: Three words for soul
hookLine: nefesh, ruach and neshamah, all tied to breath and wind

lines: MORE THAN ONE WORD FOR SOUL.
cards: Before the coffee, before the phone, there's a short prayer in the morning service that speaks about the soul; you met it in year two. It runs something like this: my God, the soul you placed in me is pure.
You created it, you formed it, you breathed it into me, and you keep it inside me. One verb jumps out. Breathed.
Not built, not installed. The prayer leans on a scene at the start of Genesis, where God bends over a figure of earth and breathes. And Hebrew has more than one word for what English calls a soul.
Today, three of them, and one verse where a breath passes between two.

teach.b: Three words. Take them one at a time, then together. First, nefesh.

In the creation story the animals are called nefesh chayah, living creatures, and so, a chapter later, is the first human. Nefesh is the whole living being: the self that gets hungry, tired and scared. Second, ruach.
In the second verse of Genesis, the King James says "the Spirit of God moved upon the face of the waters." The Hebrew under Spirit is ruach.
After the flood, when "God made a wind to pass over the earth," that wind is ruach too. Translators reach for spirit in one place and wind in another; the Hebrew holds both at once.
Third, neshamah, breath, the word the morning prayer uses. Now put them together, in Genesis chapter two: "and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life; and man became a living soul."
Breath of life: nishmat chayim, the neshamah. Living soul: nefesh chayah.

teach.h: ONE VERSE HOLDS TWO OF THEM.
teach.b: Two of the three words share one sentence, and the thing between them is a breath.
Later teachers, in the midrash and among the mystics, read these words as different sides or layers of the soul. Some readers keep it plainer. In this verse, a soul begins as something breathed in.
You can't see it, but you can hear it, and you're doing it right now.

how: In the morning service Jews say Elohai neshamah, a blessing that thanks God for the pure soul placed within; teachers in the midrash and in Jewish mysticism speak of nefesh, ruach and neshamah as layers of the soul.

games.q: what does “three words for soul” mean?
o: nefesh, ruach and neshamah: being, wind, breath
three parts of the body: heart, mind and gut
three stages of life: birth, life and death

games.q: three words for soul — tap the pairs.
p: breath, as in the breath of life

s: Hebrew has exactly one word for soul
it has several, and nefesh, ruach and neshamah all sit close to breath and wind.
in Genesis the animals are called nefesh chayah too
living creatures: the same words used for the first human a chapter later.
the morning prayer says the soul was built inside a person
it says God breathed it in.

games.q: you're translating Genesis 8:1, after the flood. the Hebrew says God sent a ruach over the earth. which English word do you choose?
games.why: the King James chose wind: "God made a wind to pass over the earth." in Genesis 1:2 the same word became Spirit.

practice: Breathe in slowly through your nose, all the way down, and let it out; then again, noticing the air arrive cool at the nostrils, the place the verse puts it.
On the third breath out, let the word neshamah ride the breath silently, then stop counting and let the breath come on its own.
If you pray, you can say the morning prayer's thought in your own way: the soul you placed in me is pure.

wordCard.voice: Three words for soul. Nefesh, a living being. Ruach, wind and spirit. Neshamah, breath. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: breath, and soul, as in nishmat chayim, the breath of life.

carryVoice: Your line: soul is breath. You're carrying it in and out right now. Three words, one breath.
